<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chromosomal architecture has played a key role in the evolution of biodiversity. Detecting structural variants (SVs) on chromosomes has informed the study of speciation, sex determination, adaptation, and some of the earliest divergences in the tree of life. Here we present a computationally non-intensive approach based on geometric morphometrics, that uses coordinate data from conserved, single-copy DNA sequences as landmarks to quantify structural disparities of focal chromosomes via primary or haploid genome assemblies across multiple species, individuals, or cell types.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Based on two approaches, we show that this ‘geno-metric’ method can be applied at micro- and macroevolutionary scales to discover and diagnose SVs. Using human X-linked single-copy genes and ultraconserved elements as genomic ‘landmarks’, we provide empirical demonstrations with amniote sex chromosomes, the
                      <jats:italic>Drosophila virilis</jats:italic>
                      group, and placental mammal genomes. Landmark-based structural disparity analysis effectively identifies chromosomal SVs and has parallels with traditional morphometrics regarding chromosome size, landmark orientation and landmark availability. Using simulations, we show that structural disparity inferred from ultraconserved elements is correlated with overall levels of chromosome evolution; an attribute which is consistent with observed disparity between and within mammalian orders. We found that the disparity patterns of SVs have significant phylogenetic signal, giving them broad importance for studying evolutionary biology. We also discuss alternative approaches that may be used to extract genomic coordinates and SV data for multi-species comparisons.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Structural disparity analysis is a reference free, whole-genome alignment free, non-pairwise comparative method that uses coordinates of single-copy genomic markers and dimensionality reduction methods to measure SVs on homologous chromosome sets. The method offers an intuitive, rapid mechanism to detect and measure SVs and consequently, offers the potential to reveal broader patterns of chromosome evolution related to expansions, contractions, rearrangements and phylogenetic history.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Quantifying structural variants in chromosomes using landmark-based disparity

                  <jats:p>
                    Inferring molecular bonds from atomic coordinates is necessary when a reliable molecular graph is unavailable. We study the contribution of explicit hydrogens to this task using BondNet, a PaiNN-based network that jointly predicts connectivity and heavy–heavy bond types. On 27,240 GEOM-DRUGS test records, exact heavy–heavy graph recovery is 99.83% for clean coordinates and 69.56% at Gaussian coordinate noise
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\sigma =0.20$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>σ</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>
                            <mml:mn>0.20</mml:mn>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                     Å. The corresponding rates on a separately selected cohort of 10,000 PubChem3D molecules are 98.43% and 64.60%. At the higher noise level, default RDKit recovers 3.64% of PubChem3D graphs exactly; a Hückel configuration examined after the initial evaluation recovers 46.73%. A heavy-only BondNet reaches 50.70% exact match on GEOM at
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:alternatives>
                        <jats:tex-math>$$\sigma =0.20$$</jats:tex-math>
                        <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>σ</mml:mi>
                            <mml:mo>=</mml:mo>
                            <mml:mn>0.20</mml:mn>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:math>
                      </jats:alternatives>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , and the explicit-H advantage persists under matched heavy-atom perturbations. An oracle model supplied with reference hydrogen counts reaches 82.03%, suggesting that hydrogen-derived valence information contributes substantially to the observed benefit. Removing H atoms from the explicit-H model at inference sharply reduces bond-type accuracy. These results highlight the difference between bond-level and complete-graph accuracy. The GEOM test set was inspected during development, and the findings do not extend to charged molecules or authentic generated geometries.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Scientific contribution</jats:bold>
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We compare explicit-H and heavy-only input under the same training schedule and use an oracle hydrogen-count control to probe the information H atoms contribute. Heavy–heavy graph metrics, a separate PubChem3D cohort, and chemically normalized baselines show where learned bond perception succeeds and where high bond-level accuracy obscures reconstruction failures.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    Light metals are gaining increasing attention in spintronics due to their advantageous properties over traditional heavy metals. This work investigates the origin of large spin torque efficiency (
                    <jats:italic>ξ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>SOT</jats:sub>
                    ) in CuNi alloys using spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance in FeNi/CuNi bilayers. Polycrystalline CuNi shows a
                    <jats:italic>ξ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>SOT</jats:sub>
                    comparable to heavy metal Pt. By controlling crystallinity, we observe a significant modulation of
                    <jats:italic>ξ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>SOT</jats:sub>
                    , as epitaxial CuNi (001) and (111) films exhibit similar but markedly lower values than their polycrystalline counterparts. This suggests that the charge-spin conversion in CuNi is strongly influenced by crystallinity and primarily dominated by extrinsic scattering. Temperature-dependent studies further support a dominant contribution from extrinsic scattering in both paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases, with minimal contribution from spin fluctuations across the Curie temperature. Our findings deepen the understanding of charge-spin interconversion in light metals and highlight their potential for spintronic applications.
                  </jats:p>
title: Crystallinity control of spin torque efficiency in CuNi alloys

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The diplonemid
                      <jats:italic>Paradiplonema papillatum</jats:italic>
                      is a marine planktonic protist with predicted complex and versatile metabolism. Investigation of carbohydrate metabolism and capacity for anaerobic life strategy revealed a disparity between its genomic and actual physiological preference. Despite possessing the genetic toolkit that should allow it to thrive in anoxic environment,
                      <jats:italic>P. papillatum</jats:italic>
                      primarily relies on aerobic metabolism, which it finely tunes in response to nutrient availability.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle serves as a key regulatory switch. The NAD
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      - and NADP
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      -dependent IDH paralogues maintain the cycle’s plasticity, as this enzyme can support both the standard oxidative TCA cycle and its reductive branch, depending on metabolic requirements. The TCA cycle provides reduced cofactors, which branches into both canonical and non-canonical pathways when nutrients are abundant. This branched respiration is supported by ubiquinones UQ
                      <jats:sub>8</jats:sub>
                      and UQ
                      <jats:sub>9</jats:sub>
                      , whose biosynthetic pathway is a mosaic of a genes of different evolutionary origins. In addition to oxidative phosphorylation,
                      <jats:italic>P. papillatum</jats:italic>
                      can synthesize ATP in the propionate cycle and the acetate:succinate coenzyme A (CoA) transferase/succinyl-CoA synthetase cycle via substrate-level phosphorylation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results highlight the complex regulation of mitochondrial metabolism in the diverse and abundant diplonemids and provide insight into the physiological strategies of marine planktonic microeukaryotes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Aerobic preference in the marine protist Paradiplonema papillatum having anaerobic genomic potential

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Non-canonical open reading frames (ncORFs) encode many microproteins that are rarely detected by mass spectrometry (MS), hindering their annotation as proteins. The properties that make them detectable in public MS repositories are poorly understood.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We analysed 7097 Ribo-seq-supported human ncORFs, 1725 of which have peptide evidence in PeptideAtlas builds, using 18 biological features and embeddings from the ESM2 protein language model (PLM) in logistic regression and ensemble classifiers (ROC-AUC 0.768 ± 0.006 over five runs). Translation uniformity across the ORF (Cumulative In-Frame Ribosome Footprint Uniformity, CIF_HBP), mammalian conservation of ORF structure (ORBLv_mammal) and predicted HLA class I-binding peptide density were top-ranked by both SHAP and permutation importance. Adding ESM2 embeddings to the three top biological features did not change ROC-AUC (0.689 in both cases; ΔAUC = 0.000 ± 0.003), possibly because ESM2 was pre-trained on much longer canonical proteins. About 90% of positives are supported by HLA immunopeptidomics alone and 99% by HLA data alone or together with non-HLA data, so the model largely reflects immunopeptidome visibility; because all ncORFs have Ribo-seq support, it predicts MS detectability conditional on translation; when whole biotypes were held out, AUC fell from 0.706 to 0.659–0.669. Of the 200 top-ranked ncORFs, 27 were identified in a Ribo-seq-guided proteogenomic study (5.26-fold over chance,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 7.2 × 10⁻
                      <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                      ) and 28 in a second, more recent dataset (6.9-fold over chance,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 1.9 × 10⁻
                      <jats:sup>16</jats:sup>
                      ; significant after Bonferroni or Holm correction for two tests).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sustained translation across the ORF and evolutionary conservation of ORF structure are statistically associated with the cumulative MS detection of ncORF microproteins, but label-source bias, the absence of protein abundance as a feature and biotype-specific patterns limit generality. These associations can help prioritise candidates for targeted proteomic discovery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Translation uniformity and evolutionary conservation are associated with microprotein mass spectrometry detectability
